pages.x: Fighting Napoleon, Britain stopped American ships trading with France and took thousands of sailors off them for its navy, saying they were British deserters. In the west, Americans blamed Britain for arming the Native nations that resisted settlers. In June 1812 Congress declared war.

Americans expected Canada to fall easily: one former president called taking it a mere matter of marching. Instead British soldiers, Canadian militia and Native allies threw back invasion after invasion. At Queenston Heights in 1812 the British general Isaac Brock was killed leading a charge, but his side won.

The Shawnee leader Tecumseh had travelled from the Great Lakes to the Gulf, urging Native nations to unite and hold on to their land. He sided with the British, helped take Detroit in 1812, and was killed at the Battle of the Thames in Upper Canada in October 1813. His dream of a Native confederacy died with him.

In August 1814 British troops marched into Washington. Dolley Madison, the president's wife, fled the President's House after making sure a portrait of George Washington was saved. That night British officers ate the dinner left on the table, then set the house and the Capitol alight, in revenge for the Americans burning York, the capital of Upper Canada.

Weeks later the British navy bombarded Fort McHenry, which guarded Baltimore, through a rainy night. Francis Scott Key, a lawyer held on a ship in the harbour, saw at dawn that the fort's huge flag still flew, and wrote a poem about it. Sung to the tune of a London club song, it became the national anthem in 1931.

Both sides were tired of a war that neither could win. On Christmas Eve 1814 diplomats in Ghent, in what is now Belgium, signed a peace that gave back everything taken and settled nothing about the sailors. News crossed the Atlantic slowly, so the fighting went on for weeks.

In January 1815, before word of the peace arrived, a British army attacked New Orleans. Andrew Jackson's mixed force of soldiers, militia, free Black volunteers, Choctaw warriors and even pirates shot it to pieces from behind earthworks. Some 2,000 British were killed, wounded or taken, against about 70 Americans. Jackson became a hero, and later president.

The war ended in a draw, but each side remembered winning: Americans felt they had won their independence a second time, Canadians that they had saved their country, and the British hardly remembered it. The real losers were the Native nations of the Great Lakes, left by their British allies to face American expansion alone.

The Star-Spangled Banner was written at Baltimore
New Orleans was fought after the peace
